(See on <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name--</hi>character; a godly mind and life; not mere reputation with man, but what a man is in the eyes of God, with whom the name and reality are one thing (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>). This alone is "good," while all else is "vanity" when made the chief end.<div eID="gen12584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ointment--</hi>used lavishly at costly banquets and peculiarly refreshing in the sultry East. The Hebrew for "name" and for "ointment," have a happy paronomasia, Sheem and Shemen. "Ointment" is fragrant only in the place where the person is whose head and garment are scented, and only for a time. The "name" given by God to His child (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>) is for ever and in all lands. So in the case of the woman who received an everlasting name from Jesus Christ, in reward for her precious ointment (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.5">Is 56:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.3-Mark.14.9">Mr 14:3-9</reference>). Jesus Christ Himself hath such a name, as the Messiah, equivalent to Anointed (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen12585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the day of [his] death, &c.--</hi>not a general censure upon God for creating man; but, connected with the previous clause, death is to him, who hath a godly name, "better" than the day of his birth; "far better," as <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Php 1:23</reference> has it. <div eID="gen12586" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8088"/><div sID="gen12587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8088"/>2. Proving that it is not a sensual enjoyment of earthly goods which is meant in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ec 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>. A thankful use of these is right, but frequent feasting Solomon had found dangerous to piety in his own case. So Job's fear (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ec 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>). The house of feasting often shuts out thoughts of God and eternity. The sight of the dead in the "house of mourning" causes "the living" to think of their own "end." <div eID="gen12587" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8091"/><div sID="gen12592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8091"/><hi type="bold">6. crackling--</hi>answers to the loud merriment of fools. It is the very fire consuming them which produces the seeming merry noise (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.5">Joe 2:5</reference>). Their light soon goes out in the black darkness. There is a paronomasia in the Hebrew, Sirim ("thorns"), Sir ("pot"). The wicked are often compared to "thorns" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.10">Na 1:10</reference>). Dried cow-dung was the common fuel in Palestine; its slowness in burning makes the quickness of a fire of thorns the more graphic, as an image of the sudden end of fools (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>). <div eID="gen12592" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8092"/><div sID="gen12593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8092"/><hi type="bold">7. oppression--</hi>recurring to the idea (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">5:8</reference>). Its connection with <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.4-Eccl.7.6">Ec 7:4-6</reference> is, the sight of "oppression" perpetrated by "fools" might tempt the "wise" to call in question God's dispensations, and imitate the folly (equivalent to "madness") described (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Ec 7:5</reference>,<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">6</reference>). Weiss, for "oppression," translates, "distraction," produced by merriment. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Ec 5:8</reference> favors English Version.<div eID="gen12593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a gift--</hi>that is, the sight of bribery in "places of judgment" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>) might cause the wise to lose their wisdom (equivalent to "heart"), (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.6">21:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">24:1</reference>, &c.). This suits the parallelism better than "a heart of gifts"; a benevolent heart, as Weiss. <div eID="gen12594" type="x-p"/>

This suits the parallelism better than "a heart of gifts"; a benevolent heart, as Weiss.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8093"/><div sID="gen12595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8093"/>8. connected with <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ec 7:7</reference>. Let the "wise" wait for "the end," and the "oppressions" which now (in "the beginning") perplex their faith, will be found by God's working to be overruled to their good. "Tribulation worketh patience" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>), which is infinitely better than "the proud spirit" that prosperity might have generated in them, as it has in fools (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference>, 3, 12-14, 17-26; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">Jas 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12595" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8097"/><div sID="gen12599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8097"/>12. Literally, (To be) in (that is, under) the shadow (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Is 30:2</reference>) of wisdom (is the same as to be) in (under) the shadow of money; wisdom no less shields one from the ills of life than money does.<div eID="gen12599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is, that--</hi>rather, "the excellency of the knowledge of wisdom giveth life," that is, life in the highest sense, here and hereafter (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2Pe 1:3</reference>). Wisdom (religion) cannot be lost as money can. It shields one in adversity, as well as prosperity; money, only in prosperity. The question in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ec 7:10</reference> implies a want of it. <div eID="gen12600" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8099"/><div sID="gen12603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8099"/><hi type="bold">14. consider--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Ec 7:13</reference>. "Consider," that is, regard it as "the work of God"; for "God has made (Hebrew, for 'set') this (adversity) also as well as the other (prosperity)." "Adversity" is one of the things which "God has made crooked," and which man cannot "make straight." He ought therefore to be "patient" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ec 7:8</reference>).<div eID="gen12603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after him--</hi>equivalent to "that man may not find anything (to blame) after God" (that is, after "considering God's work," <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Ec 7:13</reference>). Vulgate and Syriac, "against Him" (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ec 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen12604" type="x-p"/>

Holden makes <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference> the scoffing inference of the objector, and <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Ec 7:17</reference> the answer of Solomon, now repentant. So (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>) the skeptic's objection; (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>) the answer. However, "Be not righteous over much," may be taken as Solomon's words, forbidding a self-made righteousness of outward performances, which would wrest salvation from God, instead of receiving it as the gift of His grace. It is a fanatical, pharisaical righteousness, separated from God; for the "fear of God" is in antithesis to it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ec 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.1-Matt.7.9">Mt 6:1-7; 9</reference>:14; 23:23, 24; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen12609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over wise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.3">Ro 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.16">16</reference>), presumptuously self-sufficient, as if acquainted with the whole of divine truth.<div eID="gen12610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroy thyself--</hi>expose thyself to needless persecution, austerities and the wrath of God; hence to an untimely death. "Destroy thyself" answers to "perisheth" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>); "righteous over much," to "a just man." Therefore in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference> it is self-justiciary, not a truly righteous man, that is meant. <div eID="gen12611" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8102"/><div sID="gen12612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8102"/><hi type="bold">17. over much wicked--</hi>so worded, to answer to "righteous over much." For if not taken thus, it would seem to imply that we may be wicked a little. "Wicked" refers to "wicked man" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>); "die before thy time," to "prolongeth his life," antithetically. There may be a wicked man spared to "live long," owing to his avoiding gross excesses (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>). Solomon says, therefore, Be not so foolish (answering antithetically to "over wise," <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>), as to run to such excess of riot, that God will be provoked to cut off prematurely thy day of grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Ro 2:5</reference>). The precept is addressed to a sinner. Beware of aggravating thy sin, so as to make thy case desperate. It refers to the days of Solomon's "vanity" (apostasy, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>), when only such a precept would be applicable. By litotes it includes, "Be not wicked at all." <div eID="gen12612" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8113"/><div sID="gen12631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8113"/>28. Jesus Christ alone of men fully realizes the perfect ideal of "man." "Chiefest among ten thousand" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). No perfect "woman" has ever existed, not even the Virgin Mary. Solomon, in the word "thousand," alludes to his three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8114"/><div sID="gen12633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8114"/>29. The "only" way of accounting for the scarcity of even comparatively upright men and women is that, whereas God made man upright, they (men) have, &c. The only account to be "found" of the origin of evil, the great mystery of theology, is that given in Holy Writ (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.1-Gen.3.24">Ge 2:1-3:24</reference>). Among man's "inventions" was the one especially referred to in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ec 7:26</reference>, the bitter fruits of which Solomon experienced, the breaking of God's primeval marriage law, joining one man to "one" woman (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.4">Mt 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">5, 6</reference>). "Man" is singular, namely, Adam; "they," plural, Adam, Eve, and their posterity. <chapter eID="Eccl.7"/>
